variants.headline: We fall to last place among the powers
body: A porter read the new table of powers at the council door this morning. Our name sits at the bottom of {{count}}; another held that place last posting.

variants.headline: Why our own tallies can flatter us
body: We have fallen to last of {{count}}. A minister who opens a new town has every reason to put it at the top of his report. If other countries have built towns faster than we have, those same reports can make us look strong year after year while the gap grows.

variants.headline: Citizens, we are last!
body: Last of {{count}} powers, and the palace calls the tally complicated. Bread is not complicated. A wage is not complicated. A street with a watchman on it is not complicated.
Somebody in the palace collected the credit for the good years. Let them come out and collect this.

variants.headline: Last of {{count}}, and holding
body: The standings are out: last of {{count}}. One consolation. Nobody can overtake us from there.

variants.headline: {{civilization}} enters a golden age
body: A wool merchant just back from {{civilization}} says a golden age has begun there. In its capital the yards are lit after dark, and every mason in the city has work.

variants.headline: Notice from abroad: golden days in {{civilization}}
body: Letters from the capital of {{civilization}} relate that a golden age has begun there, and the letters are confident of their facts. They write of crowded markets, new building, and a court that has never seemed so pleased with itself.

variants.headline: A rival flourishes, and the balance shifts
body: {{civilization}} has begun a golden age, and a flourishing rival is a stronger rival. Prosperity that pays for festivals pays for armies just as surely.
Every envoy who sits across from them in the next years will feel the difference. Whatever answer we mean to give, we should be building it now, while the age is young.

variants.headline: The neighbor's granary is full
body: When the neighbor's granary fills, the wise count their own grain.

variants.headline: The golden age of {{civilization}} ends
body: The golden age of {{civilization}} has ended. A timber agent just back from its yards says the scaffolding is down, and the crews have gone home to their villages.

variants.headline: An age ends in {{civilization}}
body: At its height the golden age of {{civilization}} filled its markets and put confidence in its councils. Like all such ages, it was granted, never owned.
The grant is withdrawn. What {{civilization}} does with the ordinary years that follow will be the truer measure of it.

variants.headline: The record of {{civilization}}: the age is done
body: In this season the golden age of {{civilization}} came to its end, as such ages have always ended. Its stewards have closed the last storehouse, and the court keeps its hours at plainer tables. So it is set down.

variants.headline: A golden age begins at home
body: Our nation has entered a golden age, with the country at peace. A mason who kept his tools oiled through a lean winter has taken on three new hands this week, and the scaffold on the east bank is going up at last.

variants.headline: Hear it! A golden age is upon us
body: Hear it, people of the nation! A golden age is begun, and no enemy stands in the field against us! Golden days, and peace to enjoy them in! Light the lamps, and tell it to the night watch!

variants.headline: The golden age, earned
body: A golden age does not begin by accident. It follows years of steady government, honest accounts and a peace that was kept, and the nation now collects the return on all three.
Our view: spend the age on things that outlast it. That is what good years are for.

variants.headline: Sir, they call it golden
body: Sir, the capital has proclaimed a golden age, and I am told the court is delighted with itself. In my street the flour costs what it cost on Monday, and the queue at my door is as long and as short-tempered as ever.
I ask only this, and await the reply: when does golden reach the bakers?

variants.headline: The morning the age turned golden
body: In the market they were saying it by noon: good times have come, and no war on the horizon to spoil them. One fruit seller gave away her bruised apples for the joy of it, and did not stint on the good ones either.
Golden age or not, a free apple is a free apple.

variants.headline: Our golden age ends
body: The golden age has ended. At the ropewalk, the foreman has put half his crew on short days, and the night brazier is lit no longer.

variants.headline: A kettle from the golden age
body: The good age began, on one street at least, with a tinsmith finding work for a second apprentice. We hear the young man has now turned out a kettle he can put his own name to. The age is over; its kettle ought to give good service yet.

variants.headline: After the golden age, the next one
body: The golden age is over. The error now would be to mourn it longer than a day instead of starting on the next one.
Prosperity was built once, by hands no better than ours. The same work, begun again, builds it twice.

variants.headline: A golden age begins, even against {{enemies}}
body: Our nation has entered a golden age with the war against {{enemies}} unfinished. At the depot, a quartermaster hands out new boots to men who expected none.

variants.headline: Open peace talks while we can afford to walk away
body: Our golden age has begun with the army still in the field. The council should open talks with {{enemies}} while we can afford to turn down a bad offer. If another campaign drains the treasury, the other side can name its price.

variants.headline: Hear it! A golden age, even in war!
body: Hear it, people! A golden age is ours, and the war against {{enemies}} goes on! Good years, even in wartime! Let them hear it across the lines: we flourish while we fight!

variants.headline: A partner for the next dance
body: The dance teacher gave a free lesson to celebrate the golden age. With the war still on, there were more women than men. Two women watched from the doorway until one said, “I'll step on your feet if you'll step on mine.” They stayed for the next dance.

variants.headline: The national mood recovers
body: National contentment has recovered to {{happinessPercentage}} percent. A potter who had been firing only once a week says customers have finally come back for the jars they left on her shelf.

variants.headline: The national mood has picked up
body: Good news tonight. The mood in the country has lifted to {{happinessPercentage}} in every hundred. At one assembly hall, a government supporter says he can finally talk about next year's plans without being shouted down.

variants.headline: Back above half, and it shows
body: The official count says {{happinessPercentage}} in the hundred, but you could read it on the trams: fewer arguments, a longer queue at the cake shop, a busker playing something cheerful for a change.
Half the national mood is arithmetic. The other half is cake.

variants.headline: Citizens: the hard days have eased
body: Citizens: the count says {{happinessPercentage}} of us in every hundred are content, past half at last. It was earned down here, in the shops and the yards, not in the palace. Enjoy it. And when the next hard stretch comes, remember who was in charge during the last one.

variants.headline: Our nation takes up {{ideology}}
body: The government has adopted {{ideology}} as its first guiding doctrine. A magistrate read the new text aloud this morning and entered it in the court register himself.

variants.headline: A doctrine for the state
body: The state has chosen {{ideology}}, and a chosen doctrine is a public promise: here is what the government will value, and here is what it will refuse.
Allies and rivals alike will read our politics by it from this season on. The years ahead will show whether the promise was meant.

variants.headline: A doctrine descends from the capital
body: The palace has adopted {{ideology}}, and nobody below the palace was asked. Doctrine is cheap at the top, where nobody ploughs by it.
Before the banners go up, answer one question in plain words: what does {{ideology}} do for the man at the plough? This paper will wait for the answer.

variants.headline: The state takes a doctrine
body: The government has adopted {{ideology}} as the state's guiding doctrine. At the grammar school, the master has put away the primer he has taught from for years and ordered the new one from the printer. The old ways carried the nation this far; the new creed will have to carry it farther.

variants.headline: {{civilization}} abandons {{formerIdeology}} for {{ideology}}
body: The government of {{civilization}} has set aside {{formerIdeology}} for {{ideology}}. Its embassy has sent home for new seals; the old ones carried the creed it has just abandoned.

variants.headline: A major power changes its doctrine
body: One of the world's major powers has set aside {{formerIdeology}} for {{ideology}}. The dispatch reached this desk with the sender's name scratched out.

variants.headline: Our government changes doctrine
body: Our state has set aside {{formerIdeology}} for {{ideology}}. In the council lobby, ushers are stacking the old pamphlets for the pulping cart.

variants.headline: A change of doctrine recorded
body: In this season {{civilization}} set aside {{formerIdeology}} and took up {{ideology}}. The oaths at the gate were read anew, and the old formulas struck from the register. So it is recorded.

variants.headline: {{civilization}} is reduced to a single city
body: The nation of {{civilization}}, once counted among the great powers, now holds a single city. Its chancery has crated the seals of the provinces it no longer governs.

variants.headline: A major power reduced to one city
body: A major power that held several cities last season now holds one. The dispatch reached this desk with its name cut away, and the copyist left the space blank.

variants.headline: The remaining holdings of {{civilization}}
body: Cities now held: 1
Cities lost of late: {{lost}}
A great power, holding its last walls.

variants.headline: The wide lands of {{civilization}}
body: They say the roads of {{civilization}} once ran from city to city, busy with carts. Now the roads are quiet, and one city keeps the name.
An old trader said it well: a house with one room still stands, but it is not the house it was.

variants.headline: The government adopts {{policy}}
body: Our government has adopted {{policy}}. The notice went up on the council door this morning, and a shoemaker read it twice before opening his stall.

variants.headline: Notice of a new policy
body: Notice is hereby given that the government has adopted {{policy}}. The measure takes its place in the state's program. The ministers anticipate that it will serve the nation handsomely, and the ministers have been right before.

variants.headline: The lease that stayed unsigned
body: The government has adopted {{policy}}. A printer in the west ward was on the point of renting a second shop. He says he will wait until he sees what the policy does to his costs. For one landlord, the first thing the new policy brought was the return of an unsigned lease.

variants.headline: New policy, old question
body: The government has adopted {{policy}}, and the announcement is as splendid as ever. Splendid announcements do not fill bowls.
Pin one number to it before the celebrating starts: what changes at the kitchen table. Publish that number, and this paper will lead the cheering.

variants.headline: The government takes up {{branch}}
body: The government has added {{branch}} to its program, bringing the total to {{count}} policy branches. A clerk has ruled a fresh page in the council's register for the first measures.

variants.headline: New branches of statecraft open at once
body: Our government has opened several new branches of statecraft at once. A scribe has ruled fresh pages in the register, and the ink is wet on {{count}} headings.

variants.headline: Hear it! The {{branch}} branch is open
body: Hear it, people! Your government has opened the {{branch}} branch of statecraft! {{count}} branches in hand now! {{count}} branches! Your government keeps its house in order!

variants.headline: The {{branch}} branch, recorded
body: The court took up {{branch}} in this season, and the branches of its policy now number {{count}}. The scribes have left room beneath its name for the measures that will follow.

variants.headline: The mood lifts, and a trunk stays packed
body: The mood in the street has lifted to {{happinessPercentage}} out of a hundred. At a lodging house near the square, a family that had packed two trunks in the spring has unpacked one and pushed the other under the bed.

variants.headline: A quieter docket, still short of half
body: The mood has climbed to {{happinessPercentage}} out of a hundred, and the magistrate's docket shows it: two brawls and a broken window where a riot stood in the spring.

The climb has a direction, and the direction matches the government's course. The granaries are full, the watch is paid, and the carts are not being stopped in the street. The distance to half is the work left, and it is being walked, not waited for.

variants.headline: Mood update: a quieter square
body: Street temper: {{happinessPercentage}}. The square is quieter. Under half yet. Better, not safe.

variants.headline: The mood falls, and the carter takes the back lane
body: The mood has fallen to {{happiness}} out of a hundred. A carter who usually stops at the square now unloads at his customers' back doors; he says it is easier to get home that way when tempers are short.

variants.headline: Hear it! The people are angry!
body: Hear it, hear it! The mood of the nation has fallen to {{happiness}} in the hundred! Bread, work and peace of mind: the people want them back, and they want them now! Mind it, governors, mind it!

variants.headline: Below the line, and who is counting
body: The mood count has fallen to {{happiness}} percent, below the line where revolt threatens. On the east side, a cobbler has started pinning his customers' complaints above the bench. At closing time somebody always asks whether the council has come to read them yet.
The ministers should come read that wall and tell the people who wrote on it what they mean to do.

variants.headline: The mood falls, and shops close early
body: This is the national bulletin. The mood of the nation stands at {{happiness}} in every hundred tonight. Shops on the east side closed early. The council meets in the morning. Repeat: the council meets in the morning.

variants.headline: {{name}} takes up {{ideology}}
body: The nation of {{name}} has adopted {{ideology}}, its first guiding doctrine. At its court, the ushers have a new oath to administer, and the old one is already being scraped from the door.

variants.headline: A rival power takes up {{ideology}}
body: One of the world's major powers has adopted {{ideology}} as its first guiding doctrine. The dispatch reached this desk with the sender's name inked out.

variants.headline: {{name}} now shares our doctrine
body: It is a pleasure to record that {{name}} has embraced {{ideology}}, the same doctrine that guides our own state. Common convictions make easier neighbors and easier customers, and the talk at the border will be the warmer for them. We welcome the company.

variants.headline: {{name}} has a doctrine now
body: {{name}} has adopted {{ideology}}. A nation with a doctrine is a nation with a direction. A direction can be aimed.
Watch what it builds next. Doctrine names the target before any declaration does.

variants.headline: {{civilization}} takes first place among the powers
body: An exchange runner read the new standings from the steps this morning: {{civilization}} first, the name that led last season moved down a line.

variants.headline: A new power leads the reckoning
body: A new name stands at the top of the powers' table. The dispatch reached this desk with the first line cut away.

variants.headline: First place, shared
body: First in the reckoning: {{civilization}}
The lead: shared with another power
One first place, two claimants

variants.headline: Our nation stands first
body: The reckoning now places us first among the powers. First is a fact. Keeping it is a program.
Our rivals are already preparing for the next count. So should we be, and faster.

variants.headline: The nation's mood falls below half
body: The mood has fallen to {{happiness}} out of a hundred, down {{drop}} from the last reckoning. A fishmonger on the quay says customers who used to buy for the week now buy for the day.

variants.headline: Below half, and falling
body: The mood has dropped {{drop}} points to {{happiness}} in the hundred, below half. Ministers call it serious.

Serious is what a government calls a problem it did not prevent. On the east side, a mother sends her boy to the bakery at opening time, when the day-old loaves are marked down. Serious is not the word she uses.

variants.headline: The national mood, diminished
body: We are credibly informed that national contentment has fallen {{drop}} points to {{happiness}} percent, below the halfway mark. A cloth seller tells us her customers have begun asking to buy a sleeve's worth now and pay for the rest when they have the money.

variants.headline: When the pot runs low
body: When the pot runs low, the square fills up.
